entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. entry.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

link.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

entry.content:
External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

If you prefer publishing blog posts on medium.com or other external sources, starting version v0.5.0, al-folio lets you to display your external posts in the blog feed of your website! 🎉🎉

Configuring external sources of super simple. After upgrading to v0.5.0, just add the following section to your _config.yml:

external_sources:
  - name: medium.com  # name of the source (arbitrary string)
    rss_url: https://medium.com/@<your-medium-username>/feed

The example above adds your medium.com blog post feed as an external source. But you can add arbitrary RSS feeds as sources.

Any questions or suggestions? 👉 Start a discussion on GitHub!

entry.title: a post with math
entry.content:
From Policy Gradients to Reasoning LLMs: The Mathematics Behind Modern Reinforcement Learning

Subtitle: A complete derivation of policy optimization from Bellman equations to GRPO, explaining why REINFORCE, PPO, RLHF, DPO, and verifiable-reward training work — and where they fail.

Abstract

Reinforcement learning has undergone a remarkable transformation. Once confined to robotics and game-playing, policy optimization now sits at the center of how large language models are aligned, fine-tuned, and taught to reason. This article traces the mathematical thread connecting these domains: the policy gradient theorem. We begin with the Markov decision process and Bellman equations, derive the score-function estimator from first principles, and show why subtracting a baseline leaves the expected gradient unchanged. We then develop the actor–critic architecture, generalized advantage estimation, and the clipped surrogate objective of PPO — clarifying that clipping is an optimization heuristic, not a trust-region guarantee. Turning to language models, we formalize autoregressive generation as a token-level MDP and derive the RLHF objective, including the KL-regularized optimal policy that underlies both PPO-based RLHF and Direct Preference Optimization. We present GRPO as a critic-free alternative that estimates advantages from group-relative rewards, and situate RLVR as a reward paradigm rather than an algorithm. Throughout, we distinguish mathematical guarantees from empirical regularities, derive every major objective from its assumptions, and identify the failure modes — reward hacking, distribution shift, verifier exploitation — that remain active research questions.

Table of Contents

  1. Introduction: Why Policy Optimization Still Matters
  2. Part I — The Mathematical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning
    • 2.1 What is Reinforcement Learning?
    • 2.2 The Markov Decision Process
    • 2.3 Value Functions and the Bellman Equations
    • 2.4 Classical RL Algorithms
  3. Part II — Policy Gradients: The Central Mathematical Connection
    • 3.1 Parameterized Policies and the Objective
    • 3.2 Deriving the Policy Gradient Theorem
    • 3.3 The Score Function and REINFORCE
    • 3.4 Why Policy Gradients Work
    • 3.5 Baselines and Advantage Estimation
    • 3.6 Generalized Advantage Estimation
  4. Part III — From Policy Gradients to PPO
    • 4.1 The Actor–Critic Architecture
    • 4.2 Why Vanilla Policy Gradient Is Not Enough
    • 4.3 Deriving PPO
    • 4.4 PPO and Trust-Region Policy Optimization
  5. Part IV — Connecting Classical RL to Large Language Models
    • 5.1 Why an LLM Can Be Viewed as a Policy
    • 5.2 Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Post-Training
  6. Part V — RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
    • 6.1 The RLHF Pipeline
    • 6.2 Preference Modeling
    • 6.3 Reward Maximization with a KL Constraint
    • 6.4 PPO-Based RLHF
  7. Part VI — DPO: Direct Preference Optimization
    • 7.1 Why DPO Was Introduced
    • 7.2 Deriving DPO
    • 7.3 Assumptions and Limitations
    • 7.4 RLHF (PPO) vs. DPO
  8. Part VII — RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
    • 8.1 What Is RLVR?
    • 8.2 Mathematical Formulation
    • 8.3 The Challenges of RLVR
  9. Part VIII — GRPO and Group-Based Policy Optimization
    • 9.1 Motivation
    • 9.2 Deriving Group-Relative Advantages
    • 9.3 The GRPO Policy Objective
    • 9.4 GRPO Versus PPO, RLHF, DPO, and RLVR
  10. Part IX — Additional Modern Methods and Connections
  11. Part X — A Unified Mathematical View
  12. Part XI — Practical and Scientific Limitations
  13. Part XII — Reproducible Experiments and Implementation Intuition
  14. Part XIII — Open Research Questions
  15. Conclusion
  16. Glossary of Symbols and Concepts
  17. Bibliography

1. Introduction: Why Policy Optimization Still Matters

For decades, reinforcement learning occupied a peculiar position in machine learning: mathematically elegant, empirically powerful in narrow domains, yet stubbornly difficult to scale. Supervised learning offered a straightforward recipe — compute a loss, differentiate, descend. RL offered a Bellman equation and a promise of sequential decision-making, but the path from theory to practice was littered with instability, variance, and hyperparameter sensitivity.

That changed, though not in the way early RL researchers might have predicted. The breakthrough came not from robotics or game-playing but from language. In 2022, InstructGPT demonstrated that reinforcement learning from human feedback could align a 1.3B parameter language model to be preferred over a 175B model trained only with supervised learning . A technique developed for sequential decision-making had found its most consequential application in text generation.

This article argues that policy optimization provides a unifying mathematical framework connecting these seemingly disparate domains. The same score-function estimator that lets a robot learn to grasp an object also lets a language model learn to solve mathematical problems. The same advantage function that reduces variance in continuous control also reduces variance in token-level credit assignment. The same KL-regularized objective that constrains a policy from drifting too far from a reference appears, with minor modifications, in both RLHF and Direct Preference Optimization.

But unification should not be confused with identity. RLHF is not just PPO applied to text. DPO is not just RLHF with the reward model removed. GRPO is not simply PPO without a critic. Each method makes distinct assumptions, optimizes distinct objectives, and fails in distinct ways. The goal of this article is to derive these methods from their foundations, make the assumptions explicit, and clarify what is guaranteed versus what is merely observed.

Part I — The Mathematical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning

2.1 What is Reinforcement Learning?

Supervised learning assumes a dataset of input–output pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ drawn from a fixed distribution. The learning problem is to find parameters $ heta$ minimizing expected loss $\mathbb{E}{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}[\ell(f heta(x), y)]$. Unsupervised and self-supervised learning remove the labels but retain a fixed data distribution. Reinforcement learning removes the distribution itself: the data an agent sees depends on the actions it takes.

An RL agent interacts with an environment in a loop. At time $t$, the agent observes a state $s_t$, selects an action $a_t$, receives a reward $r_{t+1}$, and transitions to a new state $s_{t+1}$. The agent’s goal is to maximize cumulative reward over time. Unlike supervised learning, there is no fixed “correct” action at each state — only actions that tend to lead to higher returns. The agent must balance exploration (trying new actions to discover their effects) against exploitation (choosing actions known to yield high reward). Rewards may be delayed: a chess move that seems poor immediately might enable a winning combination ten moves later.

Consider a robot learning to manipulate an object. The state might be joint angles and object pose; actions are motor torques; reward is +1 when the object is lifted. The robot must discover, through trial and error, which sequences of torques achieve the goal. No human labels each intermediate action. The only signal is success or failure at the end.

2.2 The Markov Decision Process

The standard formalization of sequential decision-making is the Markov Decision Process (MDP): \(\mathcal{M} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma, ho_0)\) where:

  • $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space.
  • $\mathcal{A}$ is the action space.
  • $P(s’ \mid s, a)$ is the transition probability: the probability of moving to state $s’$ after taking action $a$ in state $s$.
  • $R(s, a, s’)$ is the reward function.
  • $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ is the discount factor.
  • $ ho_0(s)$ is the initial state distribution.

A policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ specifies a probability distribution over actions given a state. A trajectory $ au = (s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, \ldots)$ is generated by sampling $s_0 \sim ho_0$, then iteratively sampling $a_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s_t)$, $s_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid s_t, a_t)$, and observing reward $r_{t+1} = R(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})$.

The discounted return from time $t$ is: \(G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}\) where $T$ is the horizon (possibly infinite). For episodic tasks, the trajectory terminates at a terminal state. For continuing tasks, $T = \infty$ and $\gamma < 1$ ensures the sum converges.

The Markov property states that the future is independent of the past given the current state: $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) = P(s_{t+1} \mid s_0, a_0, \ldots, s_t, a_t)$. This is what makes the MDP tractable — the state is a sufficient statistic for predicting the future. When the agent cannot observe the full state, the problem becomes a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP), and optimal behavior may depend on the entire history of observations. Language generation is naturally partially observable in this sense: the “state” for a language model is the prompt plus the tokens generated so far.

2.3 Value Functions and the Bellman Equations

The state-value function under policy $\pi$ is the expected return starting from state $s$: \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid s_t = s]\) The action-value function is: \(Q^\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid s_t = s, a_t = a]\) The advantage function measures how much better action $a$ is than the policy’s average behavior at state $s$: \(A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)\)

The Bellman expectation equation for $V^\pi$ follows from expanding the expectation: \(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V^\pi(s') ight]\) Similarly for $Q^\pi$: \(Q^\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s') Q^\pi(s', a') ight]\)

The Bellman optimality equations define the optimal value functions $V^$ and $Q^$: \(V^*(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V^*(s') ight]\) \(Q^*(s, a) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') ight]\)

For a finite MDP with fixed policy $\pi$, the Bellman expectation equation is linear. Define the vector $V^\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}$, the reward vector $r^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s, a) R(s, a, s’)$, and the transition matrix $P^\pi(s, s’) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) P(s’ \mid s, a)$. Then: \(V^\pi = r^\pi + \gamma P^\pi V^\pi\) Rearranging: \((I - \gamma P^\pi) V^\pi = r^\pi\) \(V^\pi = (I - \gamma P^\pi)^{-1} r^\pi\)

The inverse exists whenever $\gamma < 1$, because the spectral radius of $\gamma P^\pi$ is at most $\gamma < 1$, making $I - \gamma P^\pi$ invertible.

Worked example. Consider a two-state MDP with states ${A, B}$, one action per state, deterministic transitions: $A o B$, $B o B$. Rewards: $R(A) = 1$, $R(B) = 0$. Discount $\gamma = 0.9$. Then $r^\pi = [1, 0]^T$, and $P^\pi = egin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Solving $(I - \gamma P^\pi)V = r$: \( egin{bmatrix} 1 & -0.9 \ 0 & 0.1 \end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} V(A) \ V(B) \end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) From the second row, $0.1 V(B) = 0 \Rightarrow V(B) = 0$. From the first, $V(A) - 0.9 \cdot 0 = 1 \Rightarrow V(A) = 1$. In this case, the single reward at $A$ is collected once, and $V(A) = 1$.

Dynamic programming requires knowledge of $P$ and $R$ to perform this computation. Model-free methods learn from sampled transitions instead.

2.4 Classical RL Algorithms

The major algorithmic families differ in what they learn (values, policies, or both) and whether they use the current policy (on-policy) or data from other policies (off-policy).

Dynamic programming assumes a known model. Policy evaluation computes $V^\pi$ by iterating the Bellman equation. Policy improvement constructs a new policy $\pi’(s) = \arg\max_a Q^\pi(s, a)$. Policy iteration alternates between these until convergence. Value iteration combines them into a single update: $V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s, a)[R + \gamma V_k(s’)]$.

Monte Carlo methods estimate value functions by averaging returns from sampled trajectories. For each state visited, $V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha(G_t - V(s))$. These methods are unbiased but high variance, since $G_t$ depends on all future random actions and transitions.

Temporal-Difference (TD) learning bootstraps: $V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t))$. The term $r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$ is the TD error. TD methods have lower variance than Monte Carlo but introduce bias through the bootstrapped estimate.

SARSA is an on-policy TD control method: $Q(s_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t, a_t) + \alpha(r_{t+1} + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) - Q(s_t, a_t))$. It learns the value of the policy it is following, including exploration.

Q-learning is off-policy: $Q(s_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t, a_t) + \alpha(r_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a’} Q(s_{t+1}, a’) - Q(s_t, a_t))$. It learns the optimal action-value function regardless of the behavior policy, provided all state–action pairs are visited sufficiently often.

Deep Q-Networks (DQN) approximate $Q(s, a)$ with a neural network, using experience replay and a target network to stabilize training. DQN achieved human-level performance on Atari games from pixels, but its applicability is limited to discrete action spaces and it provides no direct way to represent stochastic policies.

REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) takes a different approach: it parameterizes the policy directly and estimates the gradient of expected return using the score function . We derive this in Part II.

Actor–Critic methods combine a policy (actor) with a value function (critic). The critic estimates $V^\pi$ or $Q^\pi$ to reduce the variance of the policy gradient.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) constrains policy updates using a clipped surrogate objective, enabling multiple epochs of optimization over collected data while limiting destructive updates.

The transition from value-based to policy-based methods is motivated by several considerations. Value-based methods struggle with continuous action spaces, where the $\max$ over actions is intractable. They also learn deterministic policies, which may be suboptimal in partially observable settings where stochasticity aids exploration. Policy gradient methods optimize the policy directly and naturally handle stochastic, continuous-action policies — including the token-level policies of language models.

Part II — Policy Gradients: The Central Mathematical Connection

3.1 Parameterized Policies and the Objective

Let $\pi_ heta(a \mid s)$ be a differentiable stochastic policy with parameters $ heta$. The objective is the expected return: \(J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim p_ heta( au)}[R( au)]\) where $ au$ is a trajectory, $p_ heta( au)$ is the distribution over trajectories induced by $\pi_ heta$ and the environment dynamics, and $R( au) = \sum_t r_t$ is the trajectory return (or discounted return).

The challenge is that $ heta$ affects not only which actions are chosen but also which states are visited. The distribution over trajectories depends on $ heta$ in a complex way. Naively differentiating through the environment is impossible when the dynamics are unknown or non-differentiable. The policy gradient theorem solves this problem by expressing the gradient in a form that depends only on quantities the agent can observe.

3.2 Deriving the Policy Gradient Theorem from First Principles

We begin with the objective written as a sum over trajectories: \(J( heta) = \sum_ au p_ heta( au) R( au)\) Differentiating: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \sum_ au abla_ heta p_ heta( au) R( au)\) Apply the log-derivative identity $ abla_ heta p_ heta( au) = p_ heta( au) abla_ heta \log p_ heta( au)$: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \sum_ au p_ heta( au) abla_ heta \log p_ heta( au) R( au) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim p_ heta} \left[ R( au) abla_ heta \log p_ heta( au) ight]\)

Now factorize the trajectory probability: \(p_ heta( au) = ho_0(s_0) \prod_{t=0}^{T-1} \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\) Taking the logarithm: \(\log p_ heta( au) = \log ho_0(s_0) + \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \left[ \log \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) + \log P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) ight]\) The terms $\log ho_0(s_0)$ and $\log P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$ do not depend on $ heta$. Therefore: \( abla_ heta \log p_ heta( au) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t)\) The unknown transition probabilities disappear from the gradient expression. This is the central insight: the gradient of the log-probability of a trajectory depends only on the gradient of the log-probability of the actions taken, weighted by the return.

This yields the policy gradient theorem: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim p_ heta} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) R( au) ight]\) A more refined version uses reward-to-go $G_t$ instead of total return $R( au)$, because rewards before time $t$ do not depend on the action at time $t$: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) G_t ight]\) This version has lower variance without introducing bias.

Assumptions. The derivation assumes that $\pi_ heta(a \mid s)$ is differentiable with respect to $ heta$, that the environment dynamics and initial state distribution do not depend on $ heta$, and that we can sample trajectories from $p_ heta$. For infinite-horizon problems, an additional assumption on the state-visitation measure is needed for the discounted case to be well-defined. The exact form of the theorem also depends on whether one uses the discounted state visitation distribution or the undiscounted one; we use the discounted formulation consistent with the definition of $G_t$.

3.3 The Score Function and the REINFORCE Algorithm

The score function is $ abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s)$. It indicates how to change $ heta$ to increase the probability of action $a$ in state $s$. If $\pi_ heta(a \mid s)$ increases with $ heta_i$, the score is positive for that component; if it decreases, the score is negative.

REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) uses the sample estimate of the policy gradient : \( heta_{k+1} = heta_k + \alpha G_t abla_ heta \log \pi_{ heta_k}(a_t \mid s_t)\) This is stochastic gradient ascent on $J( heta)$. In expectation, each update moves $ heta$ in a direction of increasing expected return. The estimator is unbiased: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{g}] = abla_ heta J( heta)$.

Numerical example. Consider a Bernoulli policy over binary actions: $\pi_ heta(a=1) = \sigma( heta)$ where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. The score function for action $a$ is: \( rac{\partial}{\partial heta} \log \pi_ heta(a) = a - \sigma( heta)\) This follows from $\log \pi_ heta(1) = \log \sigma( heta)$ and $ rac{d}{d heta}\log \sigma( heta) = 1 - \sigma( heta)$, and similarly for $a=0$.

Let $ heta = 0.5$, so $\sigma( heta) \approx 0.622$. Suppose the agent samples action $a = 1$ and receives return $G = 2$. Learning rate $\alpha = 0.1$. The gradient estimate is $\hat{g} = G \cdot (a - \sigma( heta)) = 2 \cdot (1 - 0.622) = 0.756$. The update is $ heta \leftarrow 0.5 + 0.1 \cdot 0.756 = 0.576$. The probability of action 1 increases to $\sigma(0.576) \approx 0.640$.

If instead the agent sampled $a = 0$ with the same return $G = 2$, the gradient estimate would be $\hat{g} = 2 \cdot (0 - 0.622) = -1.244$, and $ heta$ would decrease to $0.376$, reducing the probability of action 1. Positive returns reinforce the sampled action; negative returns (or low positive returns when the baseline is high) suppress it.

A single update does not guarantee that $J( heta)$ increases. The policy gradient is only an expected direction; any individual step may be noisy. Convergence requires a decreasing learning rate and sufficient sampling.

3.4 Why Policy Gradients Work

The likelihood-ratio estimator is a form of stochastic gradient estimation that does not require differentiating through the environment. It treats the environment as a black box and uses only the observed actions and returns.

The bias–variance trade-off is central to understanding policy gradient methods. The REINFORCE estimator is unbiased but high variance. The return $G_t$ can vary widely across trajectories, and the score function can be large. Variance scales with the horizon length, making long-horizon problems especially difficult.

Deterministic policy gradients (Silver et al., 2014) take a different approach: for deterministic policies $\mu_ heta(s)$, the gradient involves the derivative of $Q$ with respect to actions, which requires a differentiable model or a learned critic. These methods are typically off-policy and can be more sample-efficient, but they lack the exploration benefits of stochastic policies.

3.5 Baselines and Advantage Estimation

The policy gradient estimator $ abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s) G_t$ has high variance because $G_t$ varies across trajectories. Subtracting a baseline $b(s)$ can reduce variance without introducing bias, provided the baseline does not depend on the action.

Proof. For any state-dependent baseline $b(s)$: \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_ heta(\cdot \mid s)} \left[ b(s) abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s) ight] = b(s) \sum_a \pi_ heta(a \mid s) abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s)\) Since $ abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s) = rac{ abla_ heta \pi_ heta(a \mid s)}{\pi_ heta(a \mid s)}$: \(= b(s) \sum_a abla_ heta \pi_ heta(a \mid s) = b(s) abla_ heta \sum_a \pi_ heta(a \mid s) = b(s) abla_ heta 1 = 0\) Therefore, subtracting $b(s)$ leaves the expected gradient unchanged.

The optimal baseline in terms of variance reduction is related to the value function. Using $b(s) = V^\pi(s)$ yields the advantage estimator: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_t abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) A^\pi(s_t, a_t) ight]\) where $A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)$. The advantage tells us whether an action is better or worse than the policy’s average behavior at that state. This is the actor–critic formulation: the actor (policy) is updated using advantages estimated by the critic (value function).

3.6 Generalized Advantage Estimation

Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2016) provides a family of advantage estimators that interpolate between high-bias, low-variance TD estimates and low-bias, high-variance Monte Carlo estimates .

Define the TD residual: \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) The GAE advantage is: \(\hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma, \lambda)} = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t-1} (\gamma \lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}\) When $\lambda = 0$, $\hat{A}t = \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s{t+1}) - V(s_t)$, which is a one-step TD estimate (low variance, high bias). When $\lambda = 1$, $\hat{A}t = \sum{l=0}^{T-t-1} \gamma^l r_{t+l} - V(s_t) = G_t - V(s_t)$, which is the Monte Carlo advantage estimate (unbiased but high variance).

The parameter $\lambda$ controls the bias–variance trade-off. In practice, $\lambda \approx 0.95$ is common. GAE is used in PPO to estimate advantages from collected rollouts. Terminal states are handled by setting $\delta_T = r_T - V(s_T)$ or simply truncating the sum. Value function approximation introduces additional bias: $\hat{A}_t$ is only as accurate as $V$ is.

Part III — From Policy Gradients to PPO

4.1 The Actor–Critic Architecture

Actor–critic methods combine a policy $\pi_ heta$ (the actor) with a value function $V_\phi$ (the critic). The actor is updated using the policy gradient with advantages estimated by the critic. The critic is trained to predict returns, typically by minimizing squared TD error: \(\mathcal{L}_V(\phi) = \mathbb{E} \left[ (V_\phi(s_t) - \hat{R}_t)^2 ight]\) where $\hat{R}t$ is a target, often $r_t + \gamma V\phi(s_{t+1})$ or the Monte Carlo return.

An entropy bonus encourages exploration by penalizing overly deterministic policies: \(\mathcal{L}_{ ext{entropy}} = -\mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_a \pi_ heta(a \mid s) \log \pi_ heta(a \mid s) ight]\) The combined PPO loss (to be minimized by gradient descent) is typically: \(\mathcal{L} = -\mathcal{L}^{ ext{CLIP}}( heta) + c_1 \mathcal{L}_V(\phi) - c_2 \mathcal{L}_{ ext{entropy}}\) where $c_1, c_2$ are coefficients. The policy objective $\mathcal{L}^{ ext{CLIP}}$ is maximized (hence the negative sign in the loss).

4.2 Why Vanilla Policy Gradient Is Not Enough

Vanilla policy gradient suffers from several problems. The gradient estimate is noisy, requiring many samples. A single update can move the policy far from the data-collecting policy, invalidating the advantage estimates and causing performance collapse. The step size $\alpha$ is difficult to tune: too small and learning is slow; too large and the policy oscillates or diverges.

Trust-region methods address this by constraining the size of policy updates. The natural policy gradient uses the Fisher information matrix to precondition updates. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) (Schulman et al., 2015) formalizes this as a constrained optimization problem : \(\max_ heta \mathbb{E} \left[ rac{\pi_ heta(a \mid s)}{\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}}(a \mid s)} \hat{A} ight] \quad ext{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}} \| \pi_ heta)] \leq \delta\) TRPO guarantees monotonic improvement under certain approximations, but requires computing the Fisher-vector product and solving a constrained optimization, which is computationally expensive .

4.3 Deriving PPO

PPO approximates the trust-region idea with a simpler objective. Define the likelihood ratio: \(r_t( heta) = rac{\pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}\) The clipped surrogate objective is: \(L^{ ext{CLIP}}( heta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \min\left( r_t( heta) \hat{A}_t, \operatorname{clip}(r_t( heta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_t ight) ight]\)

When the advantage is positive, the objective increases with $r_t$ but is clipped at $1+\epsilon$. The minimum prevents the policy from being rewarded for increasing $r_t$ beyond $1+\epsilon$. When the advantage is negative, the objective increases as $r_t$ decreases, but the clipped term prevents reward for decreasing $r_t$ below $1-\epsilon$. In both cases, the minimum removes the incentive to make large policy changes.

Numerical examples. Let $\epsilon = 0.2$, so the clipping interval is $[0.8, 1.2]$.

Case 1: Positive advantage. $\hat{A} = 1.0$. If $r = 1.1$, then $r\hat{A} = 1.1$ and $ ext{clip}(r)\hat{A} = 1.1$, so the minimum is $1.1$. If $r = 1.5$, then $r\hat{A} = 1.5$ but $ ext{clip}(r)\hat{A} = 1.2$, so the minimum is $1.2$. The objective no longer increases beyond $r = 1.2$.

Case 2: Negative advantage. $\hat{A} = -1.0$. If $r = 0.9$, then $r\hat{A} = -0.9$ and $ ext{clip}(r)\hat{A} = -0.9$, minimum is $-0.9$. If $r = 0.5$, then $r\hat{A} = -0.5$ but $ ext{clip}(r)\hat{A} = -0.8$, so the minimum is $-0.8$. The objective stops increasing as $r$ decreases below $0.8$.

Important clarification. Clipping limits the incentive to move the ratio outside $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$, but it does not mathematically bound the KL divergence between $\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}}$ and $\pi_ heta$. The actual KL can exceed the nominal threshold if the policy changes in directions not captured by the sampled actions. PPO is a heuristic approximation to trust-region optimization, not a strict guarantee.

PPO training typically involves:

  • Collecting a batch of trajectories using the current policy.
  • Computing advantages using GAE.
  • Optimizing the clipped objective for multiple epochs over minibatches.
  • Monitoring approximate KL and stopping early if it exceeds a threshold.

Pseudocode (PPO):

Initialize policy π_θ and value function V_φ
for iteration = 1, 2, ... do
    Collect trajectories {τ_i} using π_θ
    Compute rewards and advantages using GAE with V_φ
    for epoch = 1, ..., K do
        for minibatch in trajectories do
            Compute r_t(θ) = π_θ(a_t|s_t) / π_θ_old(a_t|s_t)
            Compute L_CLIP = min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε) A_t)
            Compute L_V = (V_φ(s_t) - R_t)^2
            Compute entropy bonus
            Update θ, φ by gradient descent on -L_CLIP + c1 L_V - c2 entropy
        end for
    end for
    Update θ_old ← θ
end for

4.4 PPO and Trust-Region Policy Optimization

TRPO solves a constrained optimization problem with a hard KL constraint. PPO replaces this with a clipped objective that is easier to optimize. The practical trade-off is clear: TRPO has stronger theoretical motivation and tends to give monotonic improvement, but is more complex to implement and computationally expensive. PPO is simpler, faster, and works well in practice, but lacks the same guarantees.

PPO clipping should not be described as “equivalent to TRPO.” It is a first-order approximation that removes the incentive for large updates without enforcing a hard constraint. The empirical success of PPO suggests that the incentive structure is often sufficient, but this is an observation, not a theorem.

Part IV — Connecting Classical RL to Large Language Models

5.1 Why an LLM Can Be Viewed as a Policy

An autoregressive language model defines a distribution over token sequences: \(\pi_ heta(y \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \pi_ heta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})\) where $x$ is the prompt (context) and $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_T)$ is the generated response.

This is structurally identical to a policy over actions. The prompt $x$ corresponds to the initial state or context. Each token $y_t$ is an action. The partial response $y_{<t}$ is the state (or observation history). The response $y$ is a trajectory. A sequence-level reward $R(x, y)$ — from a human preference, a verifier, or a learned reward model — provides the return.

The key differences from classical RL are worth noting. The “environment” is deterministic: given $x$ and $y_{<t}$, the next token is sampled from $\pi_ heta$. There is no exogenous transition dynamics. The horizon is variable: responses have different lengths. The action space is enormous: vocabulary sizes range from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands. The reward is typically sequence-level, not token-level, creating a credit assignment problem across many tokens.

The MDP abstraction for language generation is approximate. The “state” $y_{<t}$ is a complete history of generated tokens, which satisfies the Markov property trivially — the next token distribution depends only on the prompt and generated tokens. But the state space is combinatorially large, and the policy is a neural network with billions of parameters. The abstraction is useful for deriving learning algorithms, not for exact dynamic programming.

5.2 Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Post-Training

Self-supervised pretraining trains the model to predict the next token on a large corpus. The objective is: \(\mathcal{L}_{ ext{pretrain}}( heta) = -\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \pi_ heta(x_t \mid x_{<t}) ight]\) This produces a model with broad knowledge and linguistic competence but no explicit instruction-following ability.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) trains on demonstrations of desired behavior: \(\mathcal{L}_{ ext{SFT}}( heta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \pi_ heta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) ight]\) This teaches the model to imitate reference responses. It is still a form of supervised learning — the model is not optimizing a reward function, only maximizing the likelihood of demonstrations.

Preference optimization and RL-based post-training go beyond imitation. The model is trained to produce responses that score highly under a reward signal. This can involve learning a reward model from human preferences (RLHF), directly optimizing preferences (DPO), or using a verifier (RLVR).

Inference-time search and verification — Best-of-N, tree search, self-consistency — improve outputs without changing the policy. These methods sample multiple responses and select the best according to some criterion. They are complementary to training-time methods but do not update the policy’s parameters.

These stages are not interchangeable. Pretraining builds capability; SFT builds instruction-following; preference optimization and RL shape behavior according to reward signals. A model cannot learn to follow instructions through pretraining alone, and SFT alone cannot teach a model to reason through problems it cannot imitate.

Part V — RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

6.1 The RLHF Pipeline

The classical RLHF pipeline (Ouyang et al., 2022) proceeds in three stages :

  1. Supervised Fine-Tuning: A pretrained language model is fine-tuned on demonstrations of desired behavior.
  2. Reward Modeling: Human annotators compare pairs of responses to the same prompt, indicating which is preferred. A reward model $r_\phi(x, y)$ is trained to predict these preferences.
  3. Policy Optimization: The language model (policy) is fine-tuned using PPO to maximize the reward model’s score, with a KL penalty to prevent drifting too far from the SFT model.

InstructGPT demonstrated that a 1.3B parameter model trained this way was preferred by human evaluators over a 175B model trained only with SFT . This result established RLHF as a practical alignment technique.

6.2 Preference Modeling

Given pairs $(x, y_w, y_l)$ where $y_w$ is preferred over $y_l$, the Bradley–Terry model assumes: \(P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l))\) The negative log-likelihood loss for the reward model is: \(\mathcal{L}_{ ext{RM}}(\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)} \left[ \log \sigma(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)) ight]\)

The reward model is identifiable only up to an additive constant that may depend on $x$. This does not affect preference predictions, since the difference $r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)$ is invariant to prompt-dependent shifts. However, it means the absolute scale of rewards is arbitrary. Annotator disagreement, preference noise, and out-of-distribution generalization all affect reward model quality. A reward model that achieves high accuracy on held-out preference pairs may still assign high rewards to responses that humans would disprefer — a phenomenon known as reward hacking.

6.3 Reward Maximization with a KL Constraint

The RLHF objective is: \(\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)} [r_\phi(x, y)] - eta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot \mid x) \| \pi_{ ext{ref}}(\cdot \mid x))\) where $\pi_{ ext{ref}}$ is the reference policy (typically the SFT model) and $ eta$ controls the strength of the KL penalty.

For a fixed prompt $x$, the optimal policy has a closed form. Consider maximizing $\sum_y \pi(y) r(y) - eta \sum_y \pi(y) \log rac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y)}$ subject to $\sum_y \pi(y) = 1$. The Lagrangian is: \(\mathcal{L} = \sum_y \pi(y) r(y) - eta \sum_y \pi(y) \log rac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y)} + \lambda \left( 1 - \sum_y \pi(y) ight)\) Setting the derivative with respect to $\pi(y)$ to zero: \(r(y) - eta \left( \log rac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y)} + 1 ight) - \lambda = 0\) Solving: \(\pi^*(y \mid x) = rac{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp(r_\phi(x, y)/ eta)}{Z(x)}\) where $Z(x) = \sum_y \pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp(r_\phi(x, y)/ eta)$ is the partition function.

This derivation assumes that $\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x) > 0$ for all $y$ considered, and that the sum over $y$ is finite (or that the exponential tilt is integrable). The optimal policy reweights the reference distribution exponentially by reward, with temperature $ eta$.

6.4 PPO-Based RLHF

In practice, the KL-regularized objective is optimized using PPO. The reward for a response $y$ to prompt $x$ is augmented with a per-token KL penalty: \(r(x, y) = r_\phi(x, y) - eta \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left[ \log rac{\pi_ heta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})} ight]\) This penalizes tokens where the policy deviates from the reference. The sequence-level reward $r_\phi$ is propagated to tokens via the advantage estimator (typically GAE), with a learned value function providing the critic.

Credit assignment across tokens is difficult: a single sequence-level reward must be distributed across many token-level actions. The value function learns to predict the expected reward from each partial response. Reward hacking occurs when the policy discovers responses that score highly under $r_\phi$ but are not genuinely preferred by humans — a form of Goodhart’s law. Distribution shift compounds this: as the policy deviates from the data on which the reward model was trained, the reward model’s predictions become less reliable.

Part VI — DPO: Direct Preference Optimization

7.1 Why DPO Was Introduced

RLHF with PPO is complex: it requires training a reward model, sampling from the policy during training, and tuning PPO hyperparameters. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) eliminates the reward model and the online RL loop, optimizing preferences directly .

7.2 Deriving DPO from the KL-Regularized Objective

Starting from the optimal policy: \(\pi^*(y \mid x) = rac{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp(r(x, y)/ eta)}{Z(x)}\) Rearrange to express the reward: \(r(x, y) = eta \log rac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x)} + eta \log Z(x)\)

Substitute this into the Bradley–Terry model for preferences: \(P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l))\) \(= \sigma\left( eta \log rac{\pi^*(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} + eta \log Z(x) - eta \log rac{\pi^*(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} - eta \log Z(x) ight)\) The prompt-dependent term $ eta \log Z(x)$ cancels: \(= \sigma\left( eta \log rac{\pi^*(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - eta \log rac{\pi^*(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} ight)\)

Replacing the unknown $\pi^*$ with the parameterized policy $\pi_ heta$ and minimizing the negative log-likelihood of preferences yields the DPO loss: \(\mathcal{L}_{ ext{DPO}}( heta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)} \left[ \log \sigma \left( eta \log rac{\pi_ heta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - eta \log rac{\pi_ heta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} ight) ight]\)

Assumptions and limitations. DPO assumes the preference data follows the Bradley–Terry model and that the reference policy is a good approximation of the optimal policy’s support. The implicit reward $r_ heta(x, y) = eta \log rac{\pi_ heta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{ ext{ref}}(y \mid x)}$ is only defined up to a prompt-dependent constant. DPO is an offline method: it cannot explore beyond the preference data. It can be prone to over-optimization when the reference policy is weak or the data is noisy. Length and tokenization effects can introduce spurious correlations: longer responses may be preferred for reasons unrelated to quality, and DPO’s implicit reward can exploit this.

7.3 RLHF (PPO) vs. DPO

Dimension RLHF (PPO) DPO
Reward model Learned explicitly Implicit via policy ratio
Sampling Online (from current policy) Offline (fixed preference data)
Reference policy Used for KL penalty Used for implicit reward baseline
Computational cost High (reward model + PPO) Moderate (single training stage)
Stability Sensitive to hyperparameters More stable in practice
Exploration Yes, through sampling No

DPO should not be described as “the same as PPO without a critic.” It is a different objective derived from a different starting point: the closed-form solution to a KL-regularized reward maximization problem. It optimizes an implicit reward, not an explicit one, and it does so offline.

Part VII — RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

8.1 What Is RLVR?

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) replaces learned reward models with deterministic or programmatic verification. The reward is computed by a verifier: \(R(x, y) = \operatorname{Verify}(x, y)\) For mathematical problems, the verifier may check whether the final answer matches a ground-truth answer. For code, it may run unit tests. For formal reasoning, it may check proof validity .

The distinction from RLHF is the source of the reward signal: subjective human preferences versus objective verification. Verifiable rewards are low-noise and difficult to hack, provided the verifier is correct. But they are also narrow: domains without clear correctness criteria (open-ended writing, dialogue, ethical judgment) cannot be verified programmatically.

8.2 Mathematical Formulation

For a binary verifier, $R(x, y) \in {0, 1}$. The expected reward objective is: \(J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}} \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_ heta(\cdot \mid x)} [R(x, y)]\) The policy gradient is: \( abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}} \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_ heta(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ R(x, y) \sum_{t=1}^{T} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) ight]\) This is the same score-function estimator as in classical RL, with the sequence-level reward substituting for the trajectory return.

The verifier may check the final answer only, or it may verify intermediate steps. Outcome supervision provides a single reward at the end. Process supervision provides rewards for each reasoning step . Process supervision can improve credit assignment but requires step-level labels, which are expensive to obtain.

8.3 The Challenges of RLVR

Sparse rewards. Binary rewards provide no gradient signal on problems the policy always fails or always solves. Group-based methods (GRPO) address this by comparing responses within a group, but if all responses in a group receive the same reward, the relative advantage is zero.

Exploration. Verifiable rewards require the policy to occasionally produce correct solutions. If the policy’s pass@k on a problem is zero for all $k$ up to the group size, no learning signal is available. Curriculum learning and hint-based methods attempt to address this.

Multiple valid solutions. A verifier that checks only the final answer may accept incorrect reasoning that happens to reach the right result, or reject correct reasoning with a non-canonical format. Verifier design is a substantive challenge.

Reward hacking. Even deterministic verifiers can be exploited. A policy may learn to produce outputs that pass the verifier without genuinely solving the problem — for example, by memorizing answer patterns or exploiting formatting conventions. This is a form of specification gaming.

Generalization. Improvements on verifiable tasks do not automatically transfer to non-verifiable domains. A model trained on mathematics with RLVR may not become better at writing, reasoning about ethics, or engaging in open-ended dialogue.

Part VIII — GRPO and Group-Based Policy Optimization

9.1 Motivation

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024), is a critic-free alternative to PPO for language model optimization . Instead of training a value function to estimate advantages, GRPO samples multiple responses per prompt and computes relative advantages within the group.

The motivation is practical: value functions for long-horizon language generation are difficult to train accurately, and their approximation errors introduce bias into advantage estimates. Group-relative advantages avoid this by using the group itself as a baseline.

9.2 Deriving Group-Relative Advantages

For a prompt $x$, sample $G$ responses ${y_1, \ldots, y_G}$ from $\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}}$. Compute rewards $R_1, \ldots, R_G$. Define: \(\mu_R = rac{1}{G} \sum_{i=1}^{G} R_i, \quad \sigma_R = \sqrt{ rac{1}{G} \sum_{i=1}^{G} (R_i - \mu_R)^2}\) The normalized advantage for response $i$ is: \(\hat{A}_i = rac{R_i - \mu_R}{\sigma_R + \varepsilon}\) where $\varepsilon$ is a small constant for numerical stability.

Numerical example. Suppose $G = 4$ responses with rewards $(1, 1, 0, 0)$. Then $\mu_R = 0.5$. The deviations are $(0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5)$. The variance is $ rac{1}{4}(0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25) = 0.25$, so $\sigma_R = 0.5$. With $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$, the normalized advantages are $(1, 1, -1, -1)$. The two correct responses receive positive advantages; the two incorrect responses receive negative advantages.

If all responses receive the same reward (e.g., all 1 or all 0), $\sigma_R = 0$, and all advantages are zero (or undefined without $\varepsilon$). The group provides no relative signal — a key limitation of GRPO.

9.3 The GRPO Policy Objective

The token-level likelihood ratio is: \(r_{i,t}( heta) = rac{\pi_ heta(y_{i,t} \mid x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{ heta_{ ext{old}}}(y_{i,t} \mid x, y_{i,<t})}\) The GRPO objective (schematic form) is: \(\mathcal{J}_{ ext{GRPO}}( heta) = \mathbb{E} \left[ rac{1}{G} \sum_{i=1}^{G} rac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{t} \min\left( r_{i,t}( heta) \hat{A}_i, \operatorname{clip}(r_{i,t}( heta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_i ight) - eta D_{\mathrm{KL}} ight]\)

This is structurally similar to PPO, with two key differences: the advantage $\hat{A}i$ is shared across all tokens in response $i$ (since rewards are sequence-level), and no critic is used. The KL term is typically an estimator of the divergence between $\pi heta$ and $\pi_{ ext{ref}}$, computed per token.

The normalization by $ y_i $ (response length) is a design choice that affects the relative weighting of long and short responses. Different implementations may use different normalization schemes. Some variants remove length normalization entirely to avoid biasing toward longer outputs.

9.4 GRPO Versus PPO, RLHF, DPO, and RLVR

These methods should be classified along separate dimensions:

Method Algorithm Reward Source Online? Critic? Reference?
PPO (RLHF) Clipped surrogate Learned RM Yes Yes Yes (KL)
DPO Classification loss Preferences No No Yes (implicit)
GRPO Clipped surrogate Verifier or RM Yes No Yes (KL)
RLVR Reward paradigm Verifier Depends Depends Depends

RLVR describes a reward paradigm, not an optimization algorithm. GRPO describes an optimization algorithm that can be used with verifiable or learned rewards. PPO describes an optimization algorithm that is typically used with learned rewards but can in principle use any reward signal. DPO describes an offline preference-optimization objective.

A GRPO-style optimizer combined with verifiable rewards is a common configuration for reasoning models. A PPO-style optimizer with a learned reward model is the classical RLHF configuration. These are not mutually exclusive categories.

Part IX — Additional Modern Methods and Connections

10.1 RLAIF

Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback replaces human preference labels with AI-generated labels . Constitutional AI uses a set of principles to guide the AI’s critiques and revisions of its own outputs. RLAIF can scale preference data collection but inherits the limitations of the AI annotator: it may have systematic biases, and its judgments may not align with human preferences.

10.2 Process Reward Models and Outcome Reward Models

Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) assign a reward to the final answer. Process Reward Models (PRMs) assign rewards to intermediate reasoning steps . Process supervision provides denser credit assignment and can improve reasoning, but requires step-level labels. The trade-off between label cost and credit assignment accuracy is an active area of research.

10.3 Rejection Sampling and Best-of-N

Best-of-N sampling generates $N$ responses and selects the one with the highest reward according to a verifier or reward model. This improves performance at inference time without updating the policy. It is complementary to training-time methods but does not improve the policy’s underlying capability — it only selects better samples from the existing distribution.

10.4 Alternative Preference-Optimization Methods

IPO (Identity Preference Optimization) (Azar et al., 2024) derives a general objective $\Psi$PO from which DPO and RLHF are special cases, and proposes a variant that is more robust to over-optimization . KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization) uses prospect theory to define losses for desirable and undesirable outputs separately, removing the need for paired preferences . ORPO (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization) combines SFT and preference alignment into a single objective, eliminating the need for a reference model .

10.5 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

RL can be applied to agents that use tools, execute multi-step actions, and interact with environments. The challenges include partial observability (the agent may not observe the full state), large and structured action spaces (tool calls, API invocations), long-horizon credit assignment, and safety constraints. Agentic RL is an active research frontier.

10.6 Embodied AI and Robot Learning

The same policy-gradient foundations apply to robot learning. Continuous action spaces require policies that output means and variances of Gaussian distributions, or more complex distributions. Sim-to-real transfer addresses the gap between simulated training and physical deployment. Imitation learning (behavior cloning) is often used to initialize policies, with RL fine-tuning for performance. Reward engineering, sample efficiency, and safety remain challenges.

Part X — A Unified Mathematical View

Across REINFORCE, PPO, RLHF, DPO, RLVR, and GRPO, several components are shared:

  • Policy parameterization: All methods optimize a parameterized policy $\pi_ heta$.
  • Expected-return objective: The underlying goal is to maximize expected reward.
  • Score-function gradient: Policy gradient methods use $ abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta$ to estimate gradients.
  • Baselines and advantages: Variance reduction through baselines is universal.
  • Conservative updates: PPO clipping and KL regularization serve similar purposes.

What differs is:

  • Reward source: Human preferences, learned reward models, verifiers, or environment rewards.
  • Sampling regime: Online (PPO, GRPO) vs. offline (DPO).
  • Gradient estimator: Score-function vs. reparameterization (not covered here) vs. direct preference loss.
  • Critic: Required in PPO, absent in GRPO and DPO.
  • Reference model: Used in RLHF and GRPO for KL, implicit in DPO.

Not all methods are direct extensions of each other. DPO is derived from the closed-form solution to a KL-regularized problem, not from the policy gradient theorem. GRPO modifies PPO’s advantage estimation but retains the clipped surrogate. RLVR is a reward paradigm that can be combined with various optimizers. The relationships are conceptual and mathematical, not hierarchical.

Part XI — Practical and Scientific Limitations

Reward hacking occurs when the policy exploits flaws in the reward signal. Learned reward models are especially vulnerable: the policy may find adversarial examples that score highly without being genuinely good. Verifiers can be exploited if they are not robust.

Reward-model overoptimization is a related phenomenon: optimizing too hard against a learned reward model degrades true performance . The KL penalty mitigates this but does not eliminate it.

Policy drift occurs when the policy moves far from the reference distribution, reducing the reliability of reward estimates and potentially degrading capabilities. KL regularization constrains drift but trades off against reward maximization.

Sparse and noisy rewards make learning difficult. Binary verifiers provide no gradient signal on problems the policy cannot solve. Noisy human preferences introduce label noise.

High variance in policy-gradient estimates requires large batch sizes or variance-reduction techniques. Long horizons exacerbate this.

Exploration failure occurs when the policy never discovers high-reward behaviors. In language generation, this means the model never produces a correct solution to a hard problem.

Data contamination in reasoning benchmarks can inflate performance estimates. Test problems may appear in training data, making it unclear whether the model is reasoning or memorizing.

Evaluation beyond benchmark scores is essential. A model that improves on GSM8K may not be better at reasoning in general. Reward metrics can be gamed; human evaluation and adversarial testing are necessary complements.

These limitations are not merely engineering challenges. They reflect fundamental tensions in the RL formulation: the reward is a proxy for what we actually want, and optimizing a proxy too hard degrades true performance.

Part XII — Reproducible Experiments and Implementation Intuition

REINFORCE pseudocode:

Input: policy π_θ, environment, learning rate α
for episode = 1, 2, ... do
    Sample trajectory τ = (s_0, a_0, r_1, ..., s_T) using π_θ
    Compute returns G_t for each t
    Update θ ← θ + α Σ_t G_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t | s_t)
end for

Actor–Critic with GAE:

Input: policy π_θ, value function V_φ, environment
for iteration = 1, 2, ... do
    Collect trajectories
    Compute TD residuals δ_t = r_t + γ V_φ(s_{t+1}) - V_φ(s_t)
    Compute GAE advantages Â_t = Σ (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}
    Update θ using Â_t ∇_θ log π_θ
    Update φ by minimizing (V_φ(s_t) - (Â_t + V_φ(s_t)))^2
end for

DPO training:

Input: policy π_θ, reference π_ref, preference data (x, y_w, y_l), β
for batch in data do
    Compute log ratio_w = log π_θ(y_w|x) - log π_ref(y_w|x)
    Compute log ratio_l = log π_θ(y_l|x) - log π_ref(y_l|x)
    Loss = -log σ(β (log ratio_w - log ratio_l))
    Update θ by gradient descent on Loss
end for

GRPO with group-relative rewards:

Input: policy π_θ, reference π_ref, prompts, verifier, G, β
for iteration = 1, 2, ... do
    for prompt x in batch do
        Sample G responses {y_i} from π_θ_old
        Compute rewards R_i = Verify(x, y_i)
        Compute μ_R, σ_R, and Â_i = (R_i - μ_R)/(σ_R + ε)
    end for
    for epoch = 1, ..., K do
        for each response do
            Compute ratio r_{i,t} for each token
            Compute clipped surrogate with Â_i
            Compute KL with π_ref
            Update θ by gradient descent on -J_GRPO
        end for
    end for
    Update θ_old ← θ
end for

Toy example. Prompt: “What is 17 × 23?” Sample 4 responses:

  • $y_1$: “391” (correct, $R_1 = 1$)
  • $y_2$: “391” (correct, $R_2 = 1$)
  • $y_3$: “381” (incorrect, $R_3 = 0$)
  • $y_4$: “401” (incorrect, $R_4 = 0$)

$\mu_R = 0.5$, $\sigma_R = 0.5$, $\hat{A}_1 = \hat{A}_2 = 1$, $\hat{A}_3 = \hat{A}_4 = -1$. The policy is reinforced to produce “391” and suppressed from producing “381” and “401.” If the model had produced “391” in some contexts and other correct forms in others, the verifier’s normalization (e.g., stripping whitespace) would matter.

Part XIII — Open Research Questions

  1. How can policy-gradient variance be reduced for long reasoning trajectories without introducing bias?
  2. When does verifiable-reward training generalize beyond the verifier’s domain?
  3. How should process rewards be designed to balance credit assignment and label cost?
  4. How can reward hacking be detected and mitigated in practice?
  5. What is the relationship between exploration, inference-time search, and learning?
  6. Can RL improve tool use and embodied interaction robustly?
  7. How should researchers evaluate generalization rather than benchmark memorization?
  8. What are the trade-offs between offline preference optimization and online RL?

These are active research questions. The field has made substantial progress, but the fundamental tension — optimizing a proxy reward may degrade true performance — remains unresolved.

Conclusion

Policy optimization provides a mathematical language for connecting classical reinforcement learning to modern language model post-training. The score-function estimator, derived from the log-derivative identity, allows us to estimate gradients of expected return without knowing the environment’s dynamics. Baselines and advantage functions reduce variance. Trust-region and clipped objectives constrain updates. KL regularization keeps policies close to a reference. Preference models and verifiers provide reward signals when the environment does not.

The methods surveyed here — REINFORCE, PPO, RLHF, DPO, RLVR, GRPO — are not a linear progression. They are different points in a design space defined by the reward source, the sampling regime, the gradient estimator, and the constraints on policy updates. Understanding their mathematical foundations clarifies both their power and their limitations. The same framework that lets a robot learn to grasp an object lets a language model learn to solve a differential equation. The same failure mode — reward hacking — appears in both domains. And the same open question — how to specify what we actually want — remains unanswered.
